# Independent audit of the exact six-piece profile reduction

Audited the complete `candidate 92cf65df5512725a`. **PASS.** No correction identified. This is a fixed-tilt finite-complexity reduction, not a tent reduction or a proof of its remaining functional inequality.

## Fixed-knot objective and rank

The nonnegative knot heights have positive trapezoidal coefficients in the mass equation, so the feasible height polytope is bounded and closed. The first moments are linear because all abscissae are fixed. Concavity and cross-profile slope comparisons are linear inequalities. The cross-profile comparison uses the slopes of f and g rather than those of their upper half-roofs; the omitted factor one half is common, so their orders agree.

On each closed slope-order cell, the upper edge merge of the Minkowski sum has a fixed sequence. Its successive abscissae are the fixed sums of one knot from each profile, and its heights are affine in the knot heights. The initial height is the sum of the two upper left endpoint heights, including when an endpoint section is nonzero. Parallel ties merely insert a collinear intermediate vertex. Integration over the positive axial halfline is consequently affine, as are both endpoint tail integrals at the fixed thresholds. Thus selecting a cell vertex minimizing the objective is justified by a finite compact-polytope argument.

After merging all within-profile equal slopes, the retained m+1 and r+1 heights are independent coordinates before the other constraints are imposed. Every discarded knot height is recovered by the prescribed fixed-abscissa linear interpolation. A nonnegative concave profile of positive mass is positive at every interior support point, so active nonnegativity can occur only at the four endpoints. This includes profiles whose maximum is at a support endpoint.

Distinct reduced slopes within either profile are strictly ordered. Therefore active cross-profile slope equalities form an order-preserving partial matching, with at most min(m,r) independent equations. Repetitions inherited from collinear original pieces add no rank. Together with at most four mass/mean equations and z endpoint-zero equations, the nullity is at least m+r+2-z-4-min(m,r). If it were positive, a sufficiently short perturbation in both directions would preserve every active equation and all remaining strict inequalities. This contradicts cell vertexhood. The resulting max(m,r)<=2+z<=6 is therefore exact. Fixing all four endpoint heights instead leaves dimension m+r-2 and gives the claimed alternative bound six by the same count.

## Arbitrary profiles and endpoint limits

For the stipulated concave upper-semicontinuous closed profiles, the endpoint continuity assertion is valid: concavity against a fixed interior point gives the lower one-sided limit at least the endpoint value, and upper semicontinuity gives the opposite inequality. The usual interior continuity then gives uniform convergence of increasingly fine piecewise-linear interpolants on each closed interval. Height normalization and subtracting each interpolant's own mean restore exact mass and centroid; the translations tend to zero and keep the support widths fixed.

The bound max f<=2/w follows by integrating the two chords from a maximizing point to the support endpoints; nonnegative endpoint heights only increase this lower bound for the integral. Hence all replacement vertices lie in one compact rectangle. Each replacement body is exactly the convex hull of at most seven upper graph vertices and their lower reflections. A common subsequence of these finitely many padded vertices gives a Hausdorff limit, retaining both support endpoints. Area one and zero first moment pass to the limit by bounded convergence away from the convex boundary, so the limit remains full dimensional.

The upper boundary of that limit uses at most the seven limiting upper vertices. Their lower reflections cannot introduce an additional upper vertex, since all upper heights are nonnegative. Coalescing abscissae may produce a vertical supporting edge only at a support endpoint; removing its lower graph representative cannot increase the number of nonvertical upper edges. Thus the claimed six-piece bound survives the limit. The source correctly does not claim that the original endpoint heights survive this procedure: a short end segment can collapse into a larger supporting face.

Minkowski addition is continuous in Hausdorff distance. The area of its fixed-halfplane intersection, and of each endpoint body's fixed-halfplane intersection, converges by the same bounded-convergence argument outside the limiting body boundaries and cutting lines. Therefore the displayed limiting inequality (4) follows with alpha fixed throughout. No infimum-limit exchange, global minimizing body, uniform lower support width across arbitrary inputs, or angle-preserving replacement is assumed.

The final equivalence is exactly justified: any strict counterexample at one pair and one tilt has a replacement of no larger functional value with at most six pieces in each profile. Conversely such profiles are included among the original admissible profiles. The established two-piece tent theorem does not settle this six-piece class.
